newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Thai PTT starts seeking 0.05-pct sulphur diesel.
newsitem.headline: Thai PTT starts seeking 0.05-pct sulphur diesel.

text.p: Thailand's state-owned Petroleum Authority of Thailand (PTT) has started making market enquiries to import 0.05 percent sulphur diesel for use by its public buses from January 1, 1997, industry sources said on Monday.
They said PTT would need 25,000-30,000 tonnes of the very low sulphur grade every three months.
Thailand plans to use the 0.05 percent sulphur diesel grade for the whole country following a government mandate to curb air pollution, sources said.
Thailand started using 0.25 percent sulphur diesel instead of 0.5-percent material in October last year.
But market watchers said Thailand would have to pay a heavy price for the 0.05 percent diesel because it is made using more sophisticated hydrodesulphurising refining units.
They said it is easier and cheaper to switch from the 1.0 percent to 0.5 percent sulphur grade as it costs only about 20 cents per barrel more on a free-on-board (fob) basis.
It costs 30-35 cents per barrel more to upgrade from the 0.5 to 0.25-percent grade.
But the sources said PTT might have to pay double in terms of premiums on a cost-and-freight (c-and-f) basis for the 0.05 percent grade.

For example it normally pays between $1.20 and $1.50 per barrel premium, c-and-f Sri Racha, for the 0.25 percent grade, and may need to pay an additional $1.50 for the 0.05-percent grade, industry sources said.
The sources said refineries in Thailand, like Thai Oil, would be able to produce the 0.05 percent grade diesel by processing very light, low sulphur crudes, which cost more.

They said Thailand's Rayong and Star refineries would be able to produce this grade as well, but they would only start marketing it by the middle of 1997 as they do not have suitable storage facilities yet.
This forces PTT to seek imports for the time being, but the number of regional suppliers is limited.
One potential source is South Korea but it plans to start using 0.05-percent diesel by 1998, which will limit exports. South Korea aims to sell more 0.5 percent sulphur grade.
Japan will switch to the 0.05 percent grade from August next year.
In Singapore, only one refiner can produce 0.05 percent diesel, but one source said it was still developing storage for it.
The chances of importing from Algeria and Europe were slimmer now that Europe is switching to 0.05-percent from 0.2 percent grade next month.
The sources said Algerian cargoes might be absorbed by Europe as prices there are about $10.00 per tonne over values in the East.
